Employee | A | B | C | D | E | F | G | H | I | J | K
Uniform X | 82 | 74 | 42 | 59 | 60 | 73 | 94 | 98 | 62 | 36 | 50
Uniform Y | 78 | 75 | 63 | 56 | 67 | 82 | 99 | 90 | 72 | 48 | 61
(a) Give a reason why a Wilcoxon signed-rank test may be more appropriate than a t-test for investigating whether there is any evidence of a preference for one of the uniforms. [1]
(b) Carry out a Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test at the 10% significance level. [7]

(a) Find the probability generating function G_X(t) of X. [2]
Tanji also has two coins, each biased so that the probability of obtaining a head when it is thrown is 1/4. He throws the two coins at the same time. The number of heads obtained is denoted by Y.
(b) Find the probability generating function G_Y(t) of Y. [2]
The random variable Z is the sum of the number of red balls selected by Tanji and the number of heads obtained.
(c) Find the probability generating function of Z, expressing your answer as a polynomial. [3]
(d) Use the probability generating function of Z to find E(Z) and Var(Z). [5]

Farmer B grows apples of the same variety and claims that his apple trees produce a higher mass of apples per year than Farmer A's trees. The masses of apples from Farmer B's trees may be assumed to be normally distributed.
A random sample of 10 trees from Farmer B is chosen. The masses, x kg, of apples produced in a year are summarised as follows.
Σx = 152.0 Σx^2 = 2313.0
Test, at the 5% significance level, whether Farmer B's claim is justified. [6]

5 Chai packs china mugs into cardboard boxes. Chai's manager suspects that breakages occur at random times and that the number of breakages may follow a Poisson distribution. He takes a small sample of observations and finds that the number of breakages in a one-hour period has a mean of 2.4 and a standard deviation of 1.5. (a) Explain how this information tends to support the manager's suspicion. [2] The manager now takes a larger sample and claims that the numbers of breakages in a one-hour period follow a Poisson distribution. The numbers of breakages in a random sample of 180 one-hour periods are summarised in the following table.
Number of breakages | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 or more
Frequency | 21 | 33 | 46 | 31 | 23 | 16 | 10 | 0
The mean number of breakages calculated from this sample is 2.5. (b) Use the data from this larger sample to carry out a goodness of fit test, at the 10% significance level, to test the claim. [8]

questions.accessibleText: 6 [Diagram: a ring R at height h above a smooth horizontal surface; particle B hangs vertically below R; particle A on the surface moves in a horizontal circle, joined to R by a taut string.] A light inextensible string is threaded through a fixed smooth ring R which is at a height h above a smooth horizontal surface. One end of the string is attached to a particle A of mass m. The other end of the string is attached to a particle B of mass (6/7)m. The particle A moves in a horizontal circle on the surface. The particle B hangs in equilibrium below the ring and above the surface (see diagram). When A has constant angular speed ω, the angle between AR and BR is θ and the normal reaction between A and the surface is N. When A has constant angular speed (3/2)ω, the angle between AR and BR is α and the normal reaction between A and the surface is (1/2)N. (a) Show that cos θ = (4/9) cos α. [5] (b) Find N in terms of m and g and find the value of cos α. [4]

The two spheres are moving on a horizontal surface when they collide. Immediately before the collision, sphere A is travelling with speed u and its direction of motion makes an angle α with the line of centres. Sphere B is travelling with speed 2u and its direction of motion makes an angle β with the line of centres (see diagram). The coefficient of restitution between the spheres is 5/8 and α + β = 90°. (a) Find the component of the velocity of B parallel to the line of centres after the collision, giving your answer in terms of u and α. [4] The direction of motion of B after the collision is parallel to the direction of motion of A before the collision. (b) Find the value of tan α. [5]

questions.accessibleText: 4 Two particles A and B have masses km and m respectively. Particle A is at rest on a smooth horizontal surface and is exactly halfway between two fixed parallel smooth vertical walls. Particle B is moving on the surface with speed u in a direction perpendicular to the walls, and collides directly with A. The coefficient of restitution between the two particles is 0.2. As a result of the collision, the direction of motion of B is reversed. (a) Show that k > 5. [3] (b) Particle B then collides with one of the vertical walls and rebounds. The coefficient of restitution between B and the wall is 0.8. It then collides again with particle A at the instant when A collides with the other vertical wall. Find the value of k. [3]

It is given that u > 0 and k > 1. (a) Explain why, initially, the acceleration and velocity of P have opposite directions. The plane is inclined to the horizontal at an acute angle α. At time t = 0, a particle P is projected from A with speed u at an angle 2α to the plane and moves freely under gravity (see diagram). At the same time, a second particle Q is released from rest at A. Particle Q moves down the plane along the line of greatest slope. The two particles move in the same vertical plane. At time t = T, the two particles collide at point B. The length of AB is d. (a) By considering the motion of particle Q, show that T = sqrt(2d/(g sin α)). [2] (b) Find the value of α. [5]

student | A | B | C | D | E | F | G | H | I | J

[1] (b) Carry out a Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test at the 5% significance level to investigate whether, on average, there is a difference between the marks awarded by the two teachers. [7]

3 A biologist believes that the masses of a particular species of frog are normally distributed. He randomly selects 120 frogs of this species and records the mass, x, of each frog in grams. The results are summarised as follows.
mass, x | x < 210 | 210 ≤ x < 220 | 220 ≤ x < 230 | 230 ≤ x < 240 | 240 ≤ x < 250 | 250 ≤ x < 260 | x ≥ 260
observed frequency | 2 | 9 | 20 | 39 | 40 | 8 | 2
The biologist uses the masses of these 120 frogs to calculate unbiased estimates of the mean and variance of the underlying population. He calculates these as 236.5 g and 134.56 g^2 respectively. Most of the relevant expected frequencies, correct to 2 decimal places, are given in the following table. The expected frequencies have been calculated using the biologist's model.
mass, x | x < 210 | 210 ≤ x < 220 | 220 ≤ x < 230 | 230 ≤ x < 240 | 240 ≤ x < 250 | 250 ≤ x < 260 | x ≥ 260
expected frequency | 1.34 | 7.94 | 25.22 | 39.73 | 31.11 | c | d
(a) Find the value of c and the value of d. Give your answers correct to two decimal places. [2] (b) Carry out a goodness of fit test at the 5% significance level to investigate whether a normal distribution is a suitable model for the data. [7]

4 Members of a cycling club use the same circular route every week. Throughout the year, the members change between completing the route in a clockwise direction one week and completing the route in an anticlockwise direction the following week. The club captain believes that the anticlockwise route takes longer to complete on average than the clockwise route. To test this belief, the club captain selects a random sample of 10 members. Each of the 10 club members gives their personal best times, in minutes, for completing the route in both directions over the previous year. These times are as follows.
club member | A | B | C | D | E | F | G | H | I | J
clockwise | 127.1 | 129.1 | 139.3 | 151.4 | 142.5 | 123.6 | 153.4 | 129.7 | 140.9 | 137.4
anticlockwise | 131.0 | 132.1 | 147.3 | 150.0 | 144.3 | 127.3 | 153.5 | 129.9 | 140.6 | 140.3
(a) Explain the advantage of using paired samples to investigate the club captain's belief. [1] (b) Carry out a Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test at the 5% significance level to test the club captain's belief. [6] (c) State an assumption that is necessary for the test in 4(b) to be valid. [1]
